researcher: Codex parallel africa-regional-states research, integrated by Codex

sources.title: Rebecca Shumway: The Fante and the Transatlantic Slave Trade, 2011
sources.note: Publisher book description and chapter summaries; eighteenth-century coalition and Atlantic commerce. Distinguishes earlier Fante alliances from the 1868 constitutional movement.

sources.title: Christel Adick: An African contribution to the constitutional right to modern schooling 150 years ago, 2020
sources.note: Original historical analysis, PDF pages 6 to 16; Box 1 transcribes educational clauses. Schools were proposed, not a fully implemented national system.

sources.title: Constitution of the New Fante Confederacy, 24 November 1871
sources.note: Modern reproduction of primary English document and associated official correspondence. Educational wording independently corroborated in Adick Box 1. The quoted sample is historical English, not a translation into Fante.

sources.title: Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art: Asafo flag, frankaa
sources.note: Museum interpretation checked in indexed complete catalog text; membership, hen-and-chicks image, public performance and pre-1957 date. Direct page rendered little text.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art: Asafo flag by Kweku Kakanu
sources.note: Catalog record 88-10-1; red cotton damask, applique crocodile/fish and attributed possible proverb. Exact date not supplied in used excerpt, so not claimed as nineteenth-century.

sources.title: Susan Brown, Cooper Hewitt: Beware of Armed Women, 2014
sources.note: Curator on Fante asafo flags, rivalry and social commentary; pre-1957 object.

sources.title: Barbara Louise Endemaño Walker: Engendering Ghana’s Seascape, 2002
sources.note: Original archival and field research, Society & Natural Resources 15, pages 389 to 407; public abstract checked and full indexed author text available on ResearchGate. Colonial court cases begin 1898; later ownership evidence explicitly dated.

sources.title: A historical exploration of women’s production of Fante Kenkey at Yamoransa, 2024
sources.note: Original historical study; indexed abstract read, direct page failed. Used only for named town, women’s production/sale and changes through 2016, not unverified recipes or ancient origin stories.

sources.title: Marjorie H. Stewart: Borgu and Its Kingdoms, 1993
sources.note: Publisher description: region now divided between Benin and Nigeria, related kingdoms and reconstruction using oral, linguistic, archival and field evidence. Early precise technological dates not adopted from the brief description.

sources.title: Olayemi Akinwumi: Oral Tradition in Changing Political Contexts, 1998
sources.note: Publisher volume page provides original article extract: traditions linking Bussa, Nikki and Illo to sons of Kisra. Treated as traditions, not literal proof of overseas migration.

sources.title: Constanze Weise: Women and Trade in the Nupe-Borgu Region, 2020
sources.note: African Union library reproduces original scholarly abstract, Canadian Journal of African Studies 54(3), pages 459 to 477. Women as merchants, porters, provisioners and financial brokers; regional evidence identified as such.

sources.title: Olayemi Akinwumi: Princes as Highway Men, 2001
sources.note: African Union library abstract of original research; direct OpenEdition full text returned a verification page. Used only for nineteenth-century armed banditry, princely involvement and effects on caravan routes.

sources.title: Sam Nixon, Barpougouni Mardjoua and Franck N’Po Takpara: The Ashanti-Hausaland Trade Route and the Kingdom of Borgu, 2015
sources.note: Original January 2013 survey, Nyame Akuma 83, pages 48 to 61. Site visits and oral histories kept distinct; no unsupported absolute dates for surface remains.

sources.title: Dictionnaire Baatonum-Français, corrected version labeled 1 September 2017
sources.note: SIL/Webonary primary dictionary, indexed printed page 36 read. Entry bɔɔ wuro and example retained exactly. Direct PDF fetch failed; filename supplies version date, not a claim of first publication.

sources.title: Gaani festival: About the celebration and royal traditions
sources.note: Festival’s own account checked September 2026: Nikki, Sinaboko and horsemen. Describes contemporary living heritage, not evidence of an unchanged ancient ceremony.

sources.title: Usman Yusuf Bako, Mohammed Lawal Salahu and Dawood Omolumen Egbefo: Migration and resettlements in modern Borgu, 2023
sources.note: IKENGA 24(1), original research read via author-uploaded full text on ResearchGate as well as indexed journal PDF. Used for 1898 partition, 1954 merger and Kainji resettlement; uncritical origin-legend claims not adopted.

sources.title: Michael A. Gomez: The Problem with Malik Sy and the Foundation of Bundu, 1985
sources.note: Printed page 537 and abstract: eastern Senegal, Bundu chronology and changing origin accounts. Used for explicitly contextual Bundu material, not to certify the imported Tekrur record as a Bundu alias.

sources.title: Umar al-Naqar: Takrur, The History of a Name, 1969
sources.note: Same original study as medieval Takrur card. This followup uses only one short passage; combined with first sub-bundle remains below 200 words.

sources.title: Michael A. Gomez: Pragmatism in the Age of Jihad
sources.note: Original scholarly monograph, chapters 3 and 4; Maka Jiba, agriculture/commerce and Futa Toro reforms. Full university-hosted PDF read. Keep distinct regional polities and do not repeat Park’s misidentification of Bundu’s ruler as non-Muslim.

sources.title: Paul Naylor and Marion Wallace: Author of His Own Fate?, 2019
sources.note: Original research on Diallo’s surviving writings; abstract and documentary references checked. 1731 captivity and 1734 return, letters and Qur’an manuscripts.

sources.title: Thomas Bluett: The African Homeland of Ayuba Suleiman Diallo, 1734 excerpts
sources.note: National Humanities Center primary-source edition. Attributed family, schooling and naming examples; rejects author’s racist/generalizing commentary, miraculous antidotes and unsupported zoological tales.

sources.title: Mungo Park: Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa, 1799
sources.note: Primary observations from 1795 to 1797. Chapter III Koojar phrase explicitly traveler’s Latin transcription; chapter IV Faleme fishery and Koorkarany books. Used regionally, not to identify the imported Tekrur state. Shared source with Kaarta: combine budgets.

sources.title: Henry Louis Gates Jr.: On Race, and the Arts and Sciences, 2022
sources.note: American Academy of Arts & Sciences Bulletin Summer 2022, printed page 35, PDF page 37: Diallo also participated in slavery. Manuscript image could not be visually verified; no Arabic reverse-transcription attempted.

sources.title: G. Ugo Nwokeji, The Slave Trade and Culture in the Bight of Biafra, chapter 3
sources.note: Original historical research; publisher chapter summary read. Aro expansion and organization through a diaspora, 1740 to 1850.

sources.title: G. Ugo Nwokeji, Aro, in Encyclopedia of the Middle Passage
sources.note: Original scholarly encyclopedia entry, printed page 44. Oracle, settlements, incorporated outsiders and military partnerships.

sources.title: Ndu Life Njoku, The Dual Image of the Aro in Igbo Development History
sources.note: Full scholarly chapter read; use commercial transition and colonial conquest, not the chapter’s unsupported comparisons to modern geopolitics or very early foundation chronology.

sources.title: British Museum, Aro collection records
sources.note: Indexed museum collection list checked; individual object pages inaccessible. Records Af1920,1101.8 and .9 identify toy bow and arrow; .6 identifies bowl/cooking pot. Catalog gives 1901 and Arochukwu provenance.

sources.title: Okoro, Chikwendu and Udem, Arochukwu Women during the Colonial Period (2022)
sources.note: Full six-page original archival/interview study read, printed pages 39 to 44. Specific named women and projects used; racial stereotypes repeated in the introduction are not adopted.

sources.title: Harvard ELIAS, Beginning Igbo, Unit 3: Greetings and Responses
sources.note: Primary language teaching resource. Exact modern written Igbo and English gloss verified; not a historical Aro document or proof of identical Aro dialect usage.

sources.title: Joseph Ki-Zerbo and Michel Izard, From the Niger to the Volta, UNESCO General History of Africa V
sources.note: Scholarly chapter, printed pages 332 to 338; indexed original text verified. Direct PDF access failed. Distinguishes foundation traditions, eighteenth-century expansion and Massasi organization.

sources.title: David Robinson, The Holy War of Umar Tal, chapter 5: The Jihad in Karta, 1855 to 1856
sources.note: Full transcription of original scholarly study checked, especially sections A, B and E. Nioro entered 11 April 1855; do not reproduce popular 1854 simplification.

sources.title: William Gray and Staff Surgeon Dochard, Travels in Western Africa (1825)
sources.note: Primary expedition narrative of 1818 to 1821. Printed pages 299 to 318 distinguish recently conquered Khasso districts from Kaarta proper. Author’s colonial assumptions and racial judgments are not adopted.

sources.title: Eugène Mage, Voyage dans le Soudan occidental (1868), chapter V
sources.note: Primary observations dated February 1864, printed pages 112 to 123. Visits after Umarian conquest are clearly dated. Racial stereotyping in surrounding text is excluded.

sources.title: Stephanie Tolk, The Profundity of a Malian Greeting (Peace Corps, 2021)
sources.note: First-person account of service in Mali from 1998 to 2000; exact modern Bambara phrase and gloss checked. Not evidence of eighteenth-century Kaarta writing.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Imported 1815 to 1878 coastal outline extends well beyond a precise Fante territory. Broad Fante states narrative distinguishes eighteenth-century alliances from the 1868 to 1873 constitutional movement. No association with ato-trading-confederacy, which lies in southeastern Nigeria.

Verified missing; imported 1878 to 1914 geometry straddles present Benin/Nigeria, consistent with region rather than a unified state. No alias with Dendi kingdom or modern Nigerian emirate. Modern examples explicitly dated. Related courts’ Kisra stories are traditions, not verified Persian/Arab ancestry.

1715 to 1783 geometry southeast of medieval Takrur: bounding box -14.953,12.837,-10.831,15.834. Exact imported political referent unresolved. No alias proposed. Public title/overview/periods/items mark Bundu and Futa Toro as separate contextual examples; ending uncertain. Do not silently rename Bundu or assign an unsupported 1783 fall.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Decoded 1878 to 1914 feature lies in southeastern Nigeria, longitude 6.478 to 7.699 and latitude 5.278 to 6.733. Aro association is strongly probable from name, location and period, but not a verified source-label correction; public title and overview preserve uncertainty. Arochukwu at about 7.91 E lies outside imported polygon. No Fante association. Later everyday examples are explicitly colonial.

Imported 1783 to 1878 geometry spans longitude -12.512 to -6.734 and latitude 11.667 to 19.069, far too broad to treat as precise kingdom borders. Public periods distinguish Massassi independence from Umarian rule after 1855. Robinson’s source-based 11 April 1855 Nioro date preferred to popular 1854 shorthand. Origins date 1635 reflects explicitly qualified oral tradition, not a proven foundation year.
